items.body_md:
On August 10, Judge Vince Chhabria granted Meta's administrative motion for leave to serve discovery in *Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.*, No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D. Cal.), Dkt. 806 — authorizing discovery requests the court characterized as facially reasonable based on the sample RFPs and interrogatories the parties submitted. The order preserves plaintiffs' ability to challenge any individual request that "greatly exceeds" the scope of the samples, but the baseline grant is clear and unqualified. That ruling is material: it opens Meta to written discovery on the contributory-infringement amendment Judge Chhabria allowed in March, and fact discovery under the operative scheduling order closes December 18, 2026, leaving approximately four months to complete it. The same day, Dkt. 805 resolved the sealing dispute over the Dkt. 781 motion: the court granted limited redactions as specified in the Dkt. 796 declaration, but ordered Meta to file public copies of all attached documents — including entirely unredacted versions of any documents not covered by that declaration — within seven days, placing that compliance deadline on or before August 17. The transcript of Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson's August 5 hearing was docketed at Dkt. 804; it is currently restricted per General Order No. 59 pending the standard release period.

In *Hachette Book Group et al. v. Google LLC*, No. 1:26-cv-05870 (S.D.N.Y.), Judge Loretta A. Preska received the plaintiffs' reply brief at Dkt. 26, filed August 10, completing briefing on Google's letter motion for a pre-motion conference concerning a potential transfer of this action to the Northern District of California (Dkt. 21, filed August 4). Plaintiffs' opposition letter, filed August 7 by Jeffrey M. Gould of Oppenheim & Zebrak (Dkt. 25), had already closed the three-round exchange; the reply advances the transfer dispute to Judge Preska for a ruling or a conference order. The transfer question matters beyond forum logistics: Google's preferred venue is the N.D. Cal., where the parallel *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation* is already pending, and consolidation there would reshape discovery coordination and potentially dilute plaintiffs' SDNY litigation choices. The Dkt. 24 pro hac vice deficiency for Benjamin Blystad Gould — missing a California Supreme Court Certificate of Good Standing — remains a ministerial open item and carries no substantive consequence.

The remaining group members were quiet. In *Hachette v. Meta (Llama)*, No. 1:26-cv-03689 (S.D.N.Y., Judge Castel), the September 15, 2026, conference on venue and Meta's anticipated transfer motion remains the next fixed event; the competing letters on the motion-to-strike question (Dkts. 90 and 92) are before Judge Castel and unresolved. *Britannica v. OpenAI*, No. 1:26-cv-02097 (Judge Stein), and *Getty Images (US) v. Stability AI*, No. 3:25-cv-06891 (N.D. Cal., Judge Thompson), recorded no substantive movement.

The next concrete milestone across the group is Meta's seven-day deadline to file the unsealed Dkt. 781 documents in *Kadrey* — on or before August 17 — followed by Judge Preska's forthcoming disposition of the Google transfer conference request in *Hachette v. Google*.

items.lede: On August 10, the BlockFills estate filed Dkt. 561, an employment application, the first substantive docket entry since plan confirmation.
items.body_md:
On August 10, the BlockFills estate filed Dkt. 561, an employment application, the first substantive docket entry since plan confirmation.

The application's identity — which professional, which role, and at what compensation — is not disclosed in the docket metadata provided, so the specific terms cannot be confirmed without access to the filed document. What is clear from the docket type ("Employ (Application)") is that the estate is seeking court authority to retain a professional post-confirmation. In the context of where this case stands — 
Judge Thomas M. Horan confirmed the Chapter 11 plan on July 13, 2026, 122 days after the March 15 petition
 — a post-confirmation employment application is consistent with the wind-down or plan-administration phase: a plan administrator, special counsel, or distribution agent typically requires separate authorization once the confirmation order is entered, even where a professional served in an analogous capacity pre-confirmation. Whether the application is contested will govern its weight; an unopposed retention on standard terms is substantive but routine, while a disputed application or one involving unusual compensation structure would be important and contested. The distinction matters for estate economics: professional fees incurred post-confirmation are typically administrative expenses payable from the distributable estate, reducing the pool available to creditors.


McDermott ran a competitive, court-supervised sale that resulted in a purchase of substantially all BlockFills assets, with the sale funding the estates and supporting the expedited plan process.
 
Confirmation arrived faster than BlockFi (309 days), Celsius (484 days), Genesis Global (498 days), and FTX (697 days).
 With that sale closed and the plan confirmed, the principal remaining creditor-facing questions are the effective date's satisfaction of any outstanding conditions precedent, the timing and quantum of distributions, and the resolution of any disputed claims — all of which the professional engaged under Dkt. 561 may directly support. No objection deadline is visible on the face of the docket record; that deadline will run from service of the application and will govern when the court can enter an approval order.

The next concrete milestone is the hearing on, or approval of, Dkt. 561. The full application document, once accessible, will confirm the professional's identity, scope of engagement, rate structure, and any retainer — the details that determine whether this is a routine wind-down retention or something warranting closer scrutiny.

items.body_md:
On August 10, an unidentified movant filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (Dkt. 1190, N.D. Tex. Case No. 25-80109-sgj11), the second such motion in four days following Dkts. 1173 and 1181 filed August 7. The full text of Dkt. 1190 has not been pulled, so the identity of the movant, the collateral at issue, and the relief sought remain unconfirmed pending a PACER pull — confirmation would require review of the motion itself. What is clear is that lift-stay activity has accelerated in the immediate wake of plan confirmation on August 5, __[Law360](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy-authority/articles/2510100/harvest-sherwood-wins-ch-11-plan-approval)__, a predictable post-confirmation dynamic in a liquidating estate where creditors holding security interests in specific property move quickly once the plan is locked. Notices of hearing were docketed at Dkts. 1191 and 1198 on the same date; at least one of those hearings is likely associated with one or both of the pending lift-stay motions filed this week, though the docket lines do not specify which underlying motions they schedule.

Also on August 10, Dkt. 1188 reflects a withdrawal. Without the full text, the subject of the withdrawal — whether a claim, a motion, or an adversary filing — cannot be confirmed; a PACER pull of Dkt. 1188 would resolve this. Given the active lift-stay motion practice and ongoing claims trading, a withdrawal of a lift-stay motion or a related objection is the most probable candidate, but that is unverified. Five additional claim transfers were docketed by the claims agent (Dkts. 1189, 1192, 1195, 1196, 1197), continuing the pattern of secondary-market claim purchases that has run steadily through August. The mechanics are identical to the CRG Financial / Technical Truck And Trailer transfer (Dkt. 1165, filed August 7, $5,314.76): a trade creditor sells its allowed claim to a claim purchaser under Rule 3001(e)(2), with a 20-day objection window running from mailing before substitution becomes effective without further order. At the scale of this estate — with confirmed plan value anchored to more than $1 billion in antitrust litigation — individual small-balance transfers carry no meaningful recovery impact, but the volume signals active secondary-market interest in Harvest Sherwood paper in the weeks immediately following confirmation.

The next concrete milestone is September 21, 2026, when trial begins in Adversary Proceeding 25-08002, Harvest Sherwood v. Sprouts Farmers Market, before Judge Jernigan. That proceeding is the most proximate litigation event bearing on estate recovery, and any pre-trial motion practice or stipulation filed before then will carry the highest near-term materiality.

items.body_md:
On August 10, CashCall filed a further employment application, Dkt. 49, in Case No. 26-03102 before Judge Barrett Marum in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of California. The docket entry is styled as an "Employ (Application)" — the same procedural form as the Manatt, Phelps & Phillips retention filed at Dkt. 42 on August 5 — but the specific professional or firm being retained is not identified in the docket header, and no secondary reporting has surfaced confirming the identity. What can be said with certainty is that this is a second retention application distinct from the Manatt engagement and from the CRO notice filed at Dkt. 43; the substantive terms, proposed compensation, and applicant will appear in the filed application itself. Classified as substantive but, pending those details, not independently important until the identity and rate structure are confirmed — a contested or richly compensated retention in a case running on roughly $300,000 of interim DIP borrowing would carry materially different weight than a routine professional engagement.

The retention posture matters here because the estate's liquidity position is tight. 
Judge Marum limited interim DIP borrowings to $300,000 — far below the $1.3 million initially sought — and scheduled the second-day hearing for August 26, with the debtor's professionals running without approximately $290,000 budgeted for the carveout account during the interim period.
 Each new professional added to the estate's payroll competes against that same constrained carveout, and the U.S. Trustee has already demonstrated willingness to press on professional fees at the interim DIP stage. 
The debtor is represented by Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, LLP (Schuyler Carroll and Patrick DuBois) as legal counsel, Dundon Advisers, LLC (Matthew Dundon) as financial advisor, and Financial Law Group (Leslie Gladstone) as CRO.
 A third retention — whatever it covers — will need court approval and will draw scrutiny from the U.S. Trustee at or before the August 26 final DIP hearing, particularly given 
the docket's suggestion that the U.S. Trustee's and CFPB's arguments resonated with Judge Marum
 at the first-day hearing.

Dkts. 46–48 — the Schuyler Carroll pro hac vice admission and associated BNC certificates — are procedural and routine; they carry no independent weight on recovery. The next concrete milestone is the August 26 final DIP hearing, at which Judge Marum will rule on the full ~$4 million insider financing facility; the outcome will set the estate's operational runway and, correspondingly, the realistic timeline for any plan or asset monetization that determines creditor recovery.

items.body_md:
On August 10, the FTX Recovery Trust filed two omnibus objections to claims — one public (Dkt. 36106) and one sealed (Dkt. 36104), with a redacted public counterpart (Dkt. 36105) — setting a response deadline of September 10, 2026 and a hearing for September 17 at 9:30 a.m. before Judge Owens in Wilmington. The sealed filing is notable: the Trust's standard omnibus objection practice has proceeded almost entirely on the public docket, so a sealed objection with a simultaneously filed redacted version indicates the targeted claims involve confidential identifying information or settlement terms that the Trust has reason to protect from public disclosure. The grounds and claim count are not ascertainable from the public record. The public objection (Dkt. 36106) is a standard omnibus in the Trust's ongoing reconciliation campaign, which has now reached at least 186 omnibus objections across the life of the case — the September 17 hearing date aligns with the next omnibus hearing already on the calendar (August 19 is the upcoming omnibus hearing; the September date is a newly calendared session).

Also filed August 10, Kroll filed the quarterly claims register (Dkt. 36102), a routine administrative snapshot of the current state of the claims docket. Seven claim transfers appeared the same day: FTXCREDITOR, LLC transferred four separate redacted claims to Grand Teton C II, LLC (Dkts. 36093–36096) and one to itself (Dkt. 36092); Cherokee Acquisition transferred Claim No. 8231 to GreenWulf Master Fund, LP (Dkt. 36107); and Dingdingke Ltd. recorded one additional transfer (Dkt. 36090). The volume — five transfers to Grand Teton alone in a single day through FTXCREDITOR, LLC — suggests a coordinated portfolio acquisition by a secondary-market buyer consolidating positions ahead of what the Trust has signaled will be continued distributions. Individual transfer amounts are redacted and claim values are not ascertainable from the docket entries. Dkts. 36088, 36089, 36103, and 36109 are Kroll affidavits of mailing related to prior docket entries and carry no independent weight on recovery.

The sealed omnibus objection pair (Dkts. 36104/36105) is the item to watch before the September 10 objection deadline. Affected claimants who received notice but whose claims are sealed will need to respond without the benefit of a public record to compare against — a procedural asymmetry that could draw objections from claimants who argue inadequate disclosure. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 omnibus hearing before Judge Owens (Case No. 22-11068), which will address the queue of previously filed objections and any matters noticed for that session.

items.body_md:
On August 10, a motion to compel was filed in the Kahan Chapter 7 proceeding (Dkt. 359), followed the same day by Judge Bostwick's order setting a hearing on that motion (Dkt. 360).

The full text of Dkt. 359 is not in the pulled-document record, so the precise target of the compel — the relief sought and the party obligated to act — cannot be confirmed from available materials. Given where the case sits, the most probable context is Trustee Lassman's ongoing effort to enforce obligations arising from the July 17 sale order (Dkt. 343) approving the transfer of estate bitcoin and BTC wallets to PBTC Recovery Partners, LLC free and clear under § 363(f). That order was entered over Samara CR Holdings' and the Debtor's objection, and Samara and Kahan filed a notice of appeal (Dkt. 331) on July 13, followed by the amended notice (Dkt. 354) on July 31, and their Statement of Issues and Designation of Record on Appeal (Dkt. 357) on August 3. The Debtor's stay pending appeal was denied (Dkt. 348). With no stay in place, the sale order is operative and any motion to compel filed immediately after the appeal record was designated is consistent with a party — most likely the Trustee — pressing for compliance with that operative order. That reading is the most probable one on the face of the docket, but it remains unconfirmed without the Dkt. 359 text.

What is confirmed: Judge Bostwick responded to Dkt. 359 by entering Dkt. 360 the same day it was filed, setting a hearing — suggesting the Court treated the motion as meriting prompt attention. Dkt. 362 (pro hac vice, August 10) and Dkt. 361 (certificate of service, August 10) are omitted as procedural and routine. The next concrete milestone is the hearing date set by Dkt. 360; that date is not in the materials available and should be confirmed on the docket directly.

items.lede: On August 9, Judge Mary F. Walrath of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware granted Papaya Gaming's motion for a temporary injunction. The order immediately stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets and preserves the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
items.body_md:
On August 9, Judge Mary F. Walrath of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware granted Papaya Gaming's motion for a temporary injunction. 
The order immediately stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets and preserves the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
 
The relief was granted over strong opposition from Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz), whose demands Judge Walrath rejected.
 The injunction is the central near-term protection Papaya sought when it filed: without it, Firy could have moved to attach U.S. assets before recognition is adjudicated, potentially disrupting the Israeli-supervised fund structure on which any eventual recovery to claimants depends.


Judge Cote's underlying July 27 order required Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement plus approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs.
 The temporary injunction does not disturb that judgment or Papaya's pending appeal of it; it only freezes enforcement in the U.S. pending the Chapter 15 recognition hearing. For Firy as the sole material creditor, the practical consequence is that U.S.-side collection — including any post-judgment asset discovery or attachment — is halted for now. 
Under the terms Papaya presented to the Israeli court, it will transfer available cash into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with the fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 and additional tens of millions annually, constituting the potential source for claim settlement if the U.S. ruling becomes enforceable in Israel.
 The gap between that fund and the $729 million total exposure remains the defining recovery variable; the recognition hearing will be the next moment at which that gap is formally tested.

Dkts. 56 through 60 — pro hac vice orders for Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo of Latham & Watkins (on Skillz/Firy's behalf) and three further pro hac vice motions filed August 10 — confirm that Firy is assembling a full Latham team alongside its existing Weil Gotshal roster. That concentration of outside counsel on Firy's side signals active preparation for the recognition hearing, consistent with the deposition notices Skillz filed August 8 targeting Oriel Bachar, Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong (Dkts. 53–55). The next concrete milestone is the recognition hearing before Judge Walrath, at which she will determine whether to grant Chapter 15 recognition to the Israeli proceeding and whether the temporary injunction should be extended, modified, or dissolved — no date for that hearing is reflected on the docket as of this briefing.

items.body_md:
On August 10, a creditor filed Dkt. 103 — a motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee in Bankr. D.N.J. Case No. 26-18325 — alleging that Zhibiao "Kevin" Pan, Poolin's principal and sole equity holder, 
absconded from China to the U.S. with customer funds.
 That motion is the sharpest development in the case to date. Trustee appointment under 11 U.S.C. § 1104 displaces existing management and shifts control of the estate to a court-supervised fiduciary; if granted, it would remove Pan — and, by extension, the debtor's current restructuring professionals acting at his direction — from any role in administering the sale process or the liquidating plan. The allegation of pre-petition fund transfers by the principal sits squarely within § 1104(a)(1) grounds (fraud, dishonesty, gross mismanagement), making this motion substantively weightier than a routine creditor complaint.

Dkt. 104 — a motion to shorten time — was filed the same day, almost certainly tied to the trustee motion, signaling the moving creditor is pressing for an expedited hearing rather than waiting for a standard briefing schedule. Dkt. 105 and Dkt. 106 are a response and an objection, respectively, filed on the same date; their precise targets cannot be confirmed from the docket metadata alone, but given the clustering with the trustee motion, they most likely address either the trustee motion or the shorten-time request, and may indicate that the debtor or another party moved immediately to oppose. The creditor's identity is not disclosed in the docket entry or in the paywalled __[Law360 article](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy-authority/mid-cap/articles/2511097)__, which confirms the motion was filed but does not name the movant in its visible text.

The trustee motion lands at a structurally sensitive moment. The qualified-bid deadline for the West Texas auction (Pyote at $15 million; Tarbush at $37 million; combined floor $52 million from stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC) is September 8, with the auction scheduled for September 10. 
The debtors — Poolin Technology, Lonestar Dream Inc., and Lonestar Taproot LLC — are all directly or indirectly owned by Pan.
 A trustee appointment before the auction would transfer control of bid evaluation, stalking-horse negotiations, and plan drafting to an independent fiduciary, with unknown consequences for deal timing and terms already in place. Even if the motion ultimately fails, the expedited posture (Dkt. 104) means Judge O'Hagan is likely to be asked to set a prompt hearing — one that may compete with, or run directly into, the September 8 bid deadline. The next concrete milestone is the court's ruling on the motion to shorten time, which will set the hearing date for the trustee motion and determine whether this fight resolves before or after qualified bids are due.

Dkts. 101–102 — two pro hac vice admissions — are omitted as procedural and routine.

On August 10, RNDC's docket recorded Dkts. 160–168 — five pro hac vice orders (Dkts. 163–167), one additional pro hac vice appearance (Dkt. 160), two notices of appearance and request for notice (Dkts. 162 and 168), and one affidavit (Dkt. 161), together with the BNC certificate of mailing at Dkt. 159 filed August 9 — all procedural and routine, with no bearing on recovery or timing.

The substantive picture is unchanged from yesterday's edition. The lift-stay motion at Dkt. 146 — filed August 7 by an unidentified movant — remains without a docketed response. The response deadline runs on or about August 22 under S.D. Tex. Bankruptcy Local Rule 4001-1, two days before the second-day hearing before Judge Lopez on August 24. No plan supplement, amended plan, or order conditionally approving the Disclosure Statement at Dkt. 118 has appeared on the docket. The Disclosure Statement remains unapproved and is not yet soliciting votes; until Judge Lopez enters a conditional approval order, the solicitation and voting timeline cannot be set.

The next concrete milestone is the second-day hearing on August 24, 2026. Unless a stipulated order resolves Dkt. 146 before that date, the lift-stay motion will land before Judge Lopez in one of three postures: contested (if a response is filed by August 22), resolved by agreed order, or unopposed and subject to grant. A granted motion that removes estate property from the distributable pool — before any 363 sale has closed — compounds the structural gap between RNDC's disclosed asset range of $500 million to $1 billion and its $1 billion to $10 billion in liabilities, bearing directly on recovery prospects for the approximately 100,000 unsecured creditors owed more than $400 million per __[The Drinks Business](https://www.thedrinksbusiness.com/2026/08/rndc-court-filings-reveal-scale-of-distributors-financial-collapse/)__.
